overview.text: Neutrons are subatomic particles found with protons in atomic nuclei; ordinary hydrogen-1 is the exception, with a nucleus containing one proton and no neutron. A neutron has no net electric charge and is slightly more massive than a proton. Its three valence quarks are one up and two down, bound by the strong interaction; their charges add to zero. Neutron number distinguishes isotopes of the same element, which keep the same proton count but can have different properties: carbon-12 is stable, whereas carbon-14 is radioactive. Neutrons are also useful in research: neutron scattering helps scientists investigate the properties of materials.

key_facts.text: Neutrons have no net electric charge and are slightly more massive than protons.
A neutron’s three valence quarks are one up quark and two down quarks; their charges combine to make the neutron electrically neutral.
Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Carbon-12 is stable, while carbon-14 is radioactive, illustrating how differing neutron counts can accompany different isotope properties.
Neutron scattering helps researchers investigate material properties, including the shapes and sizes of crystals and molecules.
